## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{100}{0}{0}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can splitting a task across several agents cost more and deliver less than giving one agent the same resources?_

A planner that decomposes the work, coders that draft patches in parallel, and a reviewer that approves the result look like an engineering team, and the design is easy to build. Yet the handoffs introduce work of their own: workers repeat context, build on stale assumptions, return incompatible changes, and keep spending after their parent has stopped. One controller can already search alternatives in parallel and run isolated tools, so adding agents must buy something beyond concurrency. Separate task ownership and focused contexts can make a useful division of work, provided the runtime preserves evidence, bounds spending, and controls what each child may change. Delegation extends the horizon across handoffs, distributes state across workers, and passes authority down a tree, making closure at each boundary part of the cost of the split.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Estimate delegation overhead and scaling limits under explicit workload and scheduling assumptions
- Select coordination topologies from task dependencies, critical paths, and bounded spawning requirements
- Design typed task envelopes and bounded receipts separating claims, evidence, and runtime status
- Validate concurrent candidates against changed dependencies before publishing the exact checked artifact
- Explain how assumed error dependence changes ensemble evidence without making agreement a correctness guarantee
- Compose cancellation, resource reservations, and descendant authority while retaining unresolved obligations
- Evaluate delegation against a capable single-controller baseline using declared objectives and comparable resource ceilings

:::

## The Delegation Trade-Off {#sec-vol3-multiagent-need}

Consider a hypothetical authentication-module migration. One part changes an interface; another updates its callers. A coordinator could retain ownership of the whole task, using parallel searches and tests to gather evidence before preparing a patch. Alternatively, it could assign the interface and caller changes to separate workers, each able to inspect files, edit a candidate, and respond to tool feedback. The second design gives each worker a focused context and a bounded subtask. It also creates a new obligation: the caller patch must remain compatible with the interface that eventually lands, not merely the interface its worker first read.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_hsa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes, Horizon, State, and Authority, highlighted."}

*A fleet multiplies horizon, state, and authority, so every handoff must preserve closure.*
:::

That distinction defines the unit of delegation. A **delegated worker**\index{Delegated worker!definition} owns a bounded child trajectory with its own context, model-and-tool loop, task contract, and lifecycle. The original controller can also request several candidate samples and decide what to do next; those samples are parallel calls inside one trajectory, not delegated workers. The architectural change is the boundary between separately managed trajectories, whether the workers run on one machine or many.

The single-agent runtime of earlier chapters already manages context, runs isolated tools, reserves resources, and checks proposed effects outside the model, and its controller already runs candidate search and tools in parallel. Delegation keeps every one of those requirements and adds new boundaries. The design question is whether dividing control and context improves a declared task objective enough to pay for them.

### What the split buys

The first motivation is **context partitioning**\index{Context partitioning!definition}: each worker holds only the material its subtask needs. A worker responsible for the authentication interface retains the relevant contract and local test evidence without reading the caller worker's intermediate diagnostics, so each of its model invocations processes fewer tokens. The saving depends on the split. If both workers repeatedly need the full repository history, separate contexts duplicate that history instead of isolating it. Retrieval and compaction remain available to the single-controller baseline, so the comparison measures the additional benefit of separate trajectories.

The second motivation is *separate task ownership*. Workers pursue distinct investigations through several rounds of model calls and tool feedback while the coordinator handles dependencies and integration. Ownership leaves the dependencies in place: a worker that updates callers against an old interface revises its result after the interface worker returns. Independence comes from the task structure, never from role names in prompts.

The third motivation is *task-scoped authority*. Separate workers make the association between a subtask, its allowed tools, and its accessible resources explicit, so a test worker holds no publication authority. Spawning a child gives the runtime another place to apply the narrow grants and sandbox containment it already applies to one agent. The worker's outputs still carry claims and possibly hostile instructions into its parent's context, and its permitted external actions still create effects the runtime must settle.

@Tbl-vol3-delegation-matrix separates these opportunities from capabilities already present in the baseline.

| Dimension               | One controller already provides                    | Delegation adds                                                     |
|:------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Parallel work           | Concurrent candidate calls and tools               | Independently managed, multi-turn subtask trajectories              |
| Context                 | Retrieval, compaction, and selective observations  | Separate working contexts and explicit return boundaries            |
| Authority and isolation | Scoped grants and sandboxed execution              | Descendant grants and lifecycle relationships to enforce            |
| State and evidence      | Versioned artifacts and checks on proposed changes | Cross-worker dependency validation and integrated-result assessment |
| Resource control        | Admission, reservations, deadlines, and settlement | Aggregate obligations across descendants and their communication    |

: **What Delegation Adds**: The comparison preserves the capable single-controller runtime and identifies the extra boundaries a coordinated design must justify. {#tbl-vol3-delegation-matrix}

### The coordination tax

These advantages are never free, because every delegation pays the coordination tax (principle \ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}).

::: {#dfn-vol3-coordination-tax .callout-definition title="Coordination tax"}

***Coordination tax***\index{Coordination tax!definition} is the work and elapsed time a delegated design spends on handoffs rather than on the task: preparing and validating envelopes, delivering context, scheduling children, collecting receipts, and reconciling and integrating their results.

1. **Significance**: The tax enters both terms of the cost per accepted task, $C_{\text{eff}}$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task): its tokens and tool time raise $\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]$, and the part on the critical path lengthens every attempt against its deadline.
2. **Distinction**: The parallel work a split enables is the benefit; the coordination tax is what the split costs, and it grows with the number of workers and the dependencies between them.
3. **Common pitfall**: Counting only the workers' useful output. Duplicated context, reconciliation turns, and abandoned branches are billed in full.

:::

The runtime prepares and validates a task envelope, delivers inputs, schedules the child, collects its result, and integrates the evidence, and the coordinator may then spend additional turns reconciling conflicting proposals. Duplicated input tokens add to aggregate work and price-weighted cost; memory and elapsed time depend on how that work is scheduled. Compatible cached prefixes reduce physical prefill work when the serving system holds the required cache entries.

**Makespan**\index{Makespan!definition} is the elapsed time from a task's start to its last required completion, and it counts only the work and waits on the path to completion. A slow required branch delays the join, and a reconciliation step after the join adds further elapsed time. Whether a split shortens execution therefore depends on both the task dependencies and the schedule.

Amdahl's fixed-work argument gives the first screening model [@amdahl1967]. Let $T_{\mathrm{serial}}$ be the time for a fixed set of operations executed serially, with fraction $f$ perfectly divisible among $M$ equally fast workers and fraction $1-f$ remaining serial. Assume enough resources for that division and let $h(M)$ be the additional elapsed overhead, normalized by $T_{\mathrm{serial}}$. Then

$$\operatorname{Speedup}(M)=\frac{T_{\mathrm{serial}}}{T_M}=\frac{1}{(1-f)+f/M+h(M)}.$$ {#eq-vol3-multiagent-speedup}

@Eq-vol3-multiagent-speedup describes a specified work partition. Its reference $T_{\mathrm{serial}}$ is the partition executed serially, which differs from a measured single-controller baseline that already overlaps tools and candidate search; uneven branches and resource waits call for the richer schedule of @sec-vol3-multiagent-topologies. Within the model, a speedup over the serial reference requires

$$h(M)<f\left(1-\frac{1}{M}\right).$$

The right-hand side is the time saved by parallelizing the divisible work, and overhead consumes that saving. The inequality is a necessary condition on elapsed time alone; acceptance and cost enter the decision in @sec-vol3-multiagent-evaluation.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-delegation-screen
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SCREENING A FIXED WORK PARTITION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Goal: Find the integer worker count minimizing modeled elapsed time.
# │ Show: Normalized times at four, eight, and the best feasible worker count.
# │ How:  Enumerate (1-f) + f/M + a(M-1) under a finite resource ceiling.
# │ Note: Dimensionless hypothetical assumptions, not a measured comparison
# │       with an already-parallel single-controller runtime.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_ratio, fmt_int, fmt_multiple

class DelegationScreen:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    parallel_fraction = 0.8
    overhead_per_extra_worker = 0.02
    max_workers = 16

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    normalized_times = {}
    for workers in range(1, max_workers + 1):
        normalized_times[workers] = 1 - parallel_fraction + parallel_fraction / workers + overhead_per_extra_worker * (workers - 1)
    best_workers = min(normalized_times, key=normalized_times.get)
    best_time = normalized_times[best_workers]
    best_speedup = 1 / best_time
    speedup_cap = 1 / (1 - parallel_fraction)
    # Sensitivity: halve the per-worker overhead, same serial fraction.
    halved_overhead = overhead_per_extra_worker / 2
    halved_times = {}
    for workers in range(1, max_workers + 1):
        halved_times[workers] = 1 - parallel_fraction + parallel_fraction / workers + halved_overhead * (workers - 1)
    halved_best_workers = min(halved_times, key=halved_times.get)
    halved_best_speedup = 1 / halved_times[halved_best_workers]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(isinstance(max_workers, int) and max_workers >= 1, "Worker ceiling must be a positive integer")
    check(0 <= parallel_fraction <= 1, "Fraction must lie in [0, 1]")
    check(overhead_per_extra_worker >= 0, "Overhead cannot be negative")
    check(abs(normalized_times[1] - 1) < 1e-12, "Serial reference must be one")
    check(best_workers == 6, "Expected six-worker minimum under these assumptions")
    check(best_time < normalized_times[5] and best_time < normalized_times[7], "Minimum must beat adjacent integer counts")
    check(normalized_times[8] > best_time, "Additional workers should increase time here")
    check(halved_best_workers == 9, "Halved overhead should move the optimum to nine workers")
    check(best_speedup < halved_best_speedup < speedup_cap, "Halved overhead helps but stays under the serial cap")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    fraction_str = fmt_ratio(parallel_fraction, precision=2)
    overhead_str = fmt_ratio(overhead_per_extra_worker, precision=2)
    max_workers_str = fmt_int(max_workers)
    best_workers_str = fmt_int(best_workers)
    best_time_str = fmt_ratio(best_time, precision=3)
    four_time_str = fmt_ratio(normalized_times[4], precision=3)
    eight_time_str = fmt_ratio(normalized_times[8], precision=3)
    best_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(best_speedup, precision=1)
    speedup_cap_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup_cap, precision=0)
    halved_overhead_str = fmt_ratio(halved_overhead, precision=2)
    halved_best_workers_str = fmt_int(halved_best_workers)
    halved_best_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(halved_best_speedup, precision=1)
    added_workers_str = fmt_int(halved_best_workers - best_workers)
    added_speedup_str = fmt_ratio(halved_best_speedup - best_speedup, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-17-the-amdahl-limits-of-multi-agent .callout-notebook title="Screening a proposed work partition"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical fixed workload has $f=$ `{python} DelegationScreen.fraction_str` and assumed normalized overhead $h(M)=a(M-1)$ with $a=$ `{python} DelegationScreen.overhead_str`. The resource ceiling permits at most `{python} DelegationScreen.max_workers_str` workers. Which integer count minimizes modeled elapsed time?

**Math**: Evaluating the denominator of @eq-vol3-multiagent-speedup for each permitted count, four workers require `{python} DelegationScreen.four_time_str` of the serial reference time. The minimum occurs at `{python} DelegationScreen.best_workers_str` workers, requiring `{python} DelegationScreen.best_time_str`, a `{python} DelegationScreen.best_speedup_mult_str` speedup; eight workers increase the ratio to `{python} DelegationScreen.eight_time_str`, because the shrinking parallel term $f/M$ no longer pays for the added overhead. Halving the overhead coefficient to `{python} DelegationScreen.halved_overhead_str` moves the optimum to `{python} DelegationScreen.halved_best_workers_str` workers and the speedup to `{python} DelegationScreen.halved_best_speedup_mult_str`.

**Systems insight**: The serial fraction sets the ceiling and the overhead sets the useful fleet size. No worker count beats $1/(1-f)=$ `{python} DelegationScreen.speedup_cap_mult_str` here, and the best count sits near $\sqrt{f/a}$, so halving the per-handoff overhead adds `{python} DelegationScreen.added_workers_str` workers but only `{python} DelegationScreen.added_speedup_str` of speedup. Shrinking the serial planning and integration work is the larger lever. A measured single-controller baseline, which already overlaps tools, replaces the serial reference before any count is deployed.

:::

### From a faster schedule to a justified design

A migration service might value more accepted tasks before a deadline while permitting higher spend within a fixed ceiling; another might minimize cost per accepted task. A design that improves every measured axis is an unambiguous win, and a design that trades one axis for another is justified when the declared objective says so. The objective and constraints come first, before anyone sees which result favors the fleet. @Sec-vol3-multiagent-evaluation completes this decision with a hypothetical cohort that includes the cost of unsuccessful work.

The migration makes the structural obligation concrete. Separate interface and caller workers focus their investigations, and their outputs meet again at an integration boundary where compatibility and whole-task acceptance are checked. Before estimating a useful worker count, the runtime designer identifies which work can proceed independently and which evidence a successor needs. Those dependencies determine the coordination topology.

## Coordination Topologies {#sec-vol3-multiagent-topologies}

Before assigning agent roles, identify which results depend on which other results. In the hypothetical authentication-module migration `migration_task_01`, an interface worker and a caller worker inspect `repo_base_01` concurrently, yet the caller patch relies on an interface that its peer changes. Separate contexts leave that dependency in place, so the topology must make the handoffs and integration work explicit.

Three structures answer different questions. The **dependency graph**\index{Dependency graph!multi-agent definition} records which results or decisions must precede others. The **communication topology**\index{Communication topology!definition} determines where messages travel. The **supervision tree**\index{Supervision tree!definition} assigns responsibility for child lifetimes and outstanding work. A supervisor can own several children whose results depend on one another, so the supervision tree and the dependency graph are drawn separately. Keeping the three distinct prevents a routing choice from being mistaken for a correctness or lifecycle guarantee.

### Choose routing around the handoffs

@Tbl-vol3-topologies-comparison compares common arrangements. The most common, **supervisor-worker**\index{Supervisor-worker topology!definition} (also called orchestrator-worker), has one coordinator that decomposes the task, dispatches children, and integrates their receipts. The arrangements combine: a supervisor may dispatch parallel analyses, send their candidate artifacts through a validation pipeline, and track all work in a shared task store.

| Arrangement       | How work crosses a boundary                                                           | Useful when                                                              | Obligation that remains                                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Supervisor–worker | A coordinator assigns subtasks and collects bounded receipts                          | A task has separable investigations and an explicit integration decision | Bound dispatch, returned context, and the coordinator's own work     |
| Pipeline          | Each stage receives the artifacts and evidence its predecessor is required to provide | Later work depends on a sequence of transformations or checks            | Preserve stage preconditions and bound queues between stages         |
| Shared blackboard | Workers claim tasks and publish versioned artifacts through a shared store            | Different workers can contribute as dependencies become available        | Enforce claim ownership, publication rules, and dependency validity  |
| Actor messaging   | Workers hold local state and exchange addressed messages                              | Responsibilities require ongoing asynchronous interactions               | Define delivery, duplicate handling, ordering, and bounded mailboxes |

: **Coordination arrangements and their obligations**: Routing organizes handoffs; it does not establish that a result is correct or that shared resources are unconstrained. {#tbl-vol3-topologies-comparison}

A supervisor concentrates integration work and returned evidence at one place, and bounded receipts keep that workload manageable while preserving required evidence. A pipeline keeps each stage's input focused; for one item, dependent stages run in sequence, while different items overlap across stages as resources permit. A blackboard moves coordination into shared task and artifact state, where claims and publications still need rules. Actors exchange addressed messages with the peers they need, and each operation on shared state still needs its own conflict control.

Message counts depend on the protocol as well as its graph. If each of $N$ participants sends one message to every other participant in a round, there are $N(N-1)$ directed deliveries, and at $L$ tokens per delivery the round delivers $N(N-1)L$ tokens in aggregate. A coordinator with $N$ workers instead needs $2N$ deliveries for one dispatch and one receipt per worker, before retries or further exchanges. The mesh sends $(N-1)/2$ times as many deliveries, a ratio that grows with every participant added. Both counts measure what is sent, not what the receiving models read; repeated rounds, large returns, and shared-store polling can dominate a nominally sparse arrangement. @Fig-vol3-multi-agent-topologies draws the four arrangements of @tbl-vol3-topologies-comparison with these two counts and the obligation each one leaves to the runtime.

::: {#fig-vol3-multi-agent-topologies fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Four Coordination Arrangements**: Each panel shows where work crosses a boundary. A supervisor sends envelopes down and collects receipts, a pipeline passes artifacts through bounded queues, a blackboard mediates claims and versioned publications through a shared store, and actors exchange addressed messages through mailboxes. One supervisor round costs $2N$ deliveries and a full mesh round $N(N-1)$, but the line beneath each panel is the point: routing leaves an obligation in place and establishes nothing about whether a result is correct." fig-alt="Four panels. Panel a: a wide supervisor box above three worker boxes, each worker with a downward envelope arrow and an upward dashed receipt arrow, labeled 2N deliveries per round. Panel b: stage 1, stage 2, and stage 3 in a row, separated by two bounded queues drawn as three slots each. Panel c: three worker boxes sending claim and publish arrows to a shared store holding a claimed task and artifact versions 2 and 3, with dashed read arrows back. Panel d: four actor boxes, each with a mailbox, connected by three addressed messages, labeled full mesh N times N minus 1 per round. Each panel ends with an obligation line."}
![](images/svg/coordination_topologies.svg)
:::

The goal is therefore not to choose the graph with the fewest edges in isolation. It is to carry each required input and result through an explicit, bounded handoff without making every worker consume every peer's history.

### Dependencies bound the available concurrency

For a finite execution plan, model precedence with a directed acyclic graph (DAG), $G=(V,E)$. A vertex represents a bounded unit of work, which may be a delegated trajectory or a runtime-controlled integration check. An edge $(u,v)$ means that $v$ requires a declared condition on $u$ before it can proceed: an available artifact, a completed assessment, or an authorized control decision. A message saying “done” satisfies the edge only when it carries that evidence.

The scheduler tracks *unsatisfied* predecessors rather than the original in-degree. When every required predecessor condition is satisfied, a vertex becomes **dependency-ready**\index{Dependency-ready vertex!definition}, and dispatch additionally needs current authority, a valid budget reservation, and available resources. A failed predecessor blocks its successors or selects a declared recovery branch.

Acyclicity rules out cycles in the represented precedence relation only; deadlocks in unmodeled locks or queues, failed artifacts, and missing external responses remain the runtime's to detect. Iterative work enters the graph as bounded successive attempts or conditional control flow.

To estimate the scheduling limit, assume each vertex $v$ occupies one interchangeable worker slot for a fixed duration $d(v)$, including its local model and tool waits. Let $P$ be the available slots. For this model, aggregate slot-work $W$ and critical-path duration $T_{\text{crit}}$ are

$$
W=\sum_{v\in V}d(v),\qquad
T_{\text{crit}}=\max_{\pi\in\operatorname{Paths}(G)}\sum_{v\in\pi}d(v).
$$ {#eq-vol3-multiagent-dag-work}

Any schedule completing these vertices must satisfy

$$
T_{\text{finish}}\ge\max\left(\frac{W}{P},T_{\text{crit}}\right).
$$ {#eq-vol3-multiagent-dag-bound}

The work bound says that the slots must accommodate all occupied time. The path bound says that dependent durations cannot overlap. Both are lower bounds: contention, queueing, communication, and retries lengthen completion unless they are folded into $d(v)$ and the graph.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-multiagent-dag-schedule
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DEPENDENCY-LIMITED SCHEDULE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-17-critical-path-makespan-and-dag-scheduling and its table.
# │ Goal: Compare aggregate work with an attainable idealized DAG schedule.
# │ Show: Node durations, earliest starts/finishes, bounds, and speedup.
# │ How: Assumed slot durations; predecessor-max recurrence in topological order.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class DagSchedule:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Illustrative assumptions) ─────────────────────────────────
    workers = 4
    duration = {1: 20.5 * second, 2: 42 * second, 3: 42 * second, 4: 42 * second, 5: 43 * second, 6: 16.5 * second, 7: 69 * second}
    predecessors = {1: (), 2: (1,), 3: (1,), 4: (1,), 5: (2, 3), 6: (4,), 7: (5, 6)}

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Unlimited-slot earliest schedule; check capacity below) ─
    start = {}
    finish = {}
    for node in duration:
        ready = 0 * second
        for parent in predecessors[node]:
            ready = max(ready, finish[parent])
        start[node] = ready
        finish[node] = ready + duration[node]
    work = sum(duration.values(), 0 * second)
    critical = finish[7]
    work_bound = work / workers
    peak_slots = 0
    for instant in start.values():
        occupied = 0
        for node in duration:
            occupied += int(start[node] <= instant < finish[node])
        peak_slots = max(peak_slots, occupied)
    speedup = (work / critical).to("").magnitude
    slack6 = start[7] - finish[6]  # float on the only off-critical branch into v7

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Feasible capacity and the stated comparison) ──────────────
    check(work == 275 * second, "Aggregate work changed")
    check(critical == 174.5 * second, "Critical path changed")
    check(peak_slots == 3 and peak_slots <= workers, "Schedule exceeds capacity")
    check(work_bound < critical, "Work bound now dominates")
    check(1.575 < speedup < 1.585, "Displayed speedup changed")
    check(slack6 == 26.5 * second, "Slack on the v4-v6 branch changed")
    check(finish[2] == finish[3], "v2 and v3 must tie for the critical path")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    workers_str = fmt_int(workers)
    peak_slots_str = fmt_int(peak_slots)
    d1_str = fmt_time(duration[1], unit=second, precision=1)
    d2_str = fmt_time(duration[2], unit=second, precision=0)
    d5_str = fmt_time(duration[5], unit=second, precision=0)
    d6_str = fmt_time(duration[6], unit=second, precision=1)
    d7_str = fmt_time(duration[7], unit=second, precision=0)
    start1_str = fmt_time(start[1], unit=second, precision=0)
    start2_str = fmt_time(start[2], unit=second, precision=1)
    start5_str = fmt_time(start[5], unit=second, precision=1)
    start7_str = fmt_time(start[7], unit=second, precision=1)
    finish6_str = fmt_time(finish[6], unit=second, precision=0)
    work_str = fmt_time(work, unit=second, precision=0)
    critical_str = fmt_time(critical, unit=second, precision=1)
    work_bound_str = fmt_time(work_bound, unit=second, precision=2)
    speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup, precision=2)
    slack6_str = fmt_time(slack6, unit=second, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-17-critical-path-makespan-and-dag-scheduling .callout-notebook title="DAG scheduling in multi-agent execution"}

**Problem**: Consider an illustrative repository upgrade with `{python} DagSchedule.workers_str` worker slots. @Tbl-vol3-multiagent-dag-schedule gives assumed durations for a single successful execution of each node. Each node occupies one slot; there are no additional dispatch delays, resource conflicts, retries, or transfer costs. How much can overlap?

| Work                                                | Required predecessors | Slot duration                      | Earliest start                    | Earliest finish                     |
|:----------------------------------------------------|:----------------------|:-----------------------------------|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------|
| $v_1$: prepare shared specification                 | None                  | `{python} DagSchedule.d1_str`      | `{python} DagSchedule.start1_str` | `{python} DagSchedule.start2_str`   |
| $v_2,v_3,v_4$: refactor separate modules            | $v_1$, for each       | `{python} DagSchedule.d2_str` each | `{python} DagSchedule.start2_str` | `{python} DagSchedule.start5_str`   |
| $v_5$: assess the joint changes from two modules    | $v_2,v_3$             | `{python} DagSchedule.d5_str`      | `{python} DagSchedule.start5_str` | `{python} DagSchedule.start7_str`   |
| $v_6$: prepare bindings for the remaining module    | $v_4$                 | `{python} DagSchedule.d6_str`      | `{python} DagSchedule.start5_str` | `{python} DagSchedule.finish6_str`  |
| $v_7$: integrate and run required regression checks | $v_5,v_6$             | `{python} DagSchedule.d7_str`      | `{python} DagSchedule.start7_str` | `{python} DagSchedule.critical_str` |

: **An idealized dependency schedule**: Starts are the latest finish among required predecessors. The schedule assumes that each predecessor supplies the result required by its successor. {#tbl-vol3-multiagent-dag-schedule}

**Math**: Summing the node durations as in @eq-vol3-multiagent-dag-work gives `{python} DagSchedule.work_str` of aggregate slot-work. Dividing by the slot count gives the work term in @eq-vol3-multiagent-dag-bound, `{python} DagSchedule.work_bound_str`. The paths $v_1\to v_2\to v_5\to v_7$ and $v_1\to v_3\to v_5\to v_7$ tie for the critical path. The table's schedule uses at most `{python} DagSchedule.peak_slots_str` slots, so it is feasible under the stated capacity and attains the path bound.

**Result**: Completion takes `{python} DagSchedule.critical_str`, a `{python} DagSchedule.speedup_mult_str` speedup over executing these same nodes serially. The earlier finish of $v_6$ does not release $v_7$ while $v_5$ is unfinished. More slots cannot shorten the remaining chain under this duration model.

**Systems insight**: Only the critical path is worth shortening, and slots beyond peak concurrency buy nothing. The branch through $v_4$ and $v_6$ finishes `{python} DagSchedule.slack6_str` before $v_7$ can start, so speeding it up changes completion by zero. Shortening $v_5$ or $v_7$ saves one second of completion per second removed, up to that `{python} DagSchedule.slack6_str` of slack, while shortening $v_2$ alone saves nothing because $v_3$ ties it. The same reading applies to a measured trace: find the path, then spend engineering effort only on its vertices.

:::

### Static plans and dynamic spawning

A **static plan**\index{Static plan!definition} declares its possible stages and dependencies before execution, including conditional branches, skipped stages, and bounded retries. Its handoffs are inspectable in advance, and a worst-case resource bound follows once the work and repetition inside each stage are bounded too.

**Dynamic spawning**\index{Dynamic spawning!definition} creates additional child assignments in response to observations. A migration worker might discover an undocumented caller and request a focused investigation. The model proposes that assignment; the runtime admits it under the current task contract. Dynamic decomposition adapts the work to discoveries, at the cost of a final task set that is known only after execution. When the model alone decides how many children to spawn, that cost can dominate the task.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-multiagent-research-report
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SOURCED FIGURES FROM A MULTI-AGENT RESEARCH SYSTEM REPORT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: \ref{ws-vol3-multiagent-research-fanout-2025} and
# │          \ref{nbk-17-token-multiplier-break-even}.
# │ Goal: Hold the report's published figures in one place.
# │ Show: Early fan-out, token multiples over chat, and the evaluation gain.
# │ How: Constants quoted from @anthropic2025multiagent; no derivation here.
# │ Note: Reported by the system's builders on their own internal evaluation.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class ResearchReport:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Quoted from anthropic2025multiagent) ────────────────────
    early_subagents = 50  # subagents spawned for simple queries in early versions
    single_agent_tokens_vs_chat = 4  # "about 4x more tokens than chat"
    multi_agent_tokens_vs_chat = 15  # "about 15x more tokens than chats"
    eval_gain = 0.902  # multi-agent over single-agent, internal research eval

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (None: quoted values) ─────────────────────────────────

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Transcription sanity) ─────────────────────────────────
    check(multi_agent_tokens_vs_chat > single_agent_tokens_vs_chat > 1, "Token multiples must be ordered")
    check(0 < eval_gain < 1, "Relative gain transcribed as a fraction")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    early_subagents_str = fmt_int(early_subagents)
    single_vs_chat_mult_str = fmt_multiple(single_agent_tokens_vs_chat, precision=0)
    multi_vs_chat_mult_str = fmt_multiple(multi_agent_tokens_vs_chat, precision=0)
    eval_gain_str = fmt_percent(eval_gain, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#ws-vol3-multiagent-research-fanout-2025 .callout-war-story title="Unbounded fan-out in a multi-agent research system (2025)"}

**Context**: Anthropic's engineering team described building a research system in which a lead agent plans a query, spawns subagents that search in parallel, and synthesizes their findings [@anthropic2025multiagent].

**Mechanism**: The lead agent decided how many subagents to create. Early versions spawned `{python} ResearchReport.early_subagents_str` subagents for simple queries, searched endlessly for nonexistent sources, and had subagents distract one another with excessive updates.

**Impact**: The team reports that agents typically use about `{python} ResearchReport.single_vs_chat_mult_str` more tokens than chat interactions and multi-agent systems about `{python} ResearchReport.multi_vs_chat_mult_str` more. The multi-agent configuration outperformed a single agent by `{python} ResearchReport.eval_gain_str` on the team's internal research evaluation, so the fan-out bought real capability at a large multiple of the spend.

**Fix**: The team embedded explicit scaling rules in the lead agent's prompts, matching the number of subagents and tool calls to query complexity, from one agent for simple fact-finding upward. It also reported that the lead agent waits for each set of subagents to finish before proceeding, which simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks.

**Systems lesson**: Fan-out is a resource decision, and a model left to make it alone can overspend badly on easy tasks. Scaling rules in a prompt guide the proposal; the runtime still has to bound breadth, depth, and aggregate reservation at admission, because token multiples enter the numerator of $C_{\text{eff}}$ directly.

:::

The research system's early failure is the admission problem in miniature: the model chose the fan-out, and the fix lived in the model's prompt. Admission must bound aggregate commitments. Giving each child a budget smaller than its parent's is insufficient if many siblings receive overlapping claims on the same remaining funds. Use the harness's serialized reservation accounting: before admitting a child, atomically reserve its bounded liability against actual consumption, existing reservations, and protected finalization capacity. Parent-local work and descendant work draw on the same governed allocation without double-counting or reusing reserved funds. Unknown final charges remain outstanding rather than being refunded merely because a child timed out.

Bound fan-out, active concurrency, recursion depth, and deadlines separately: a shallow tree can still be too broad, and a concurrency cap alone leaves the number of sequential children unbounded. Declaring a child also assigns a runtime owner for its result, cancellation, and unresolved effects, which outlive the parent model call that proposed it. @Sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure develops that lifecycle obligation, while @sec-vol3-multiagent-authority distinguishes narrowing permissions from allocating consumable budgets.

The supervision tree also fixes what the runtime restarts when a child fails. Erlang/OTP supervisors make that choice an explicit per-supervisor policy [@armstrong2007erlang]. Under `one_for_one`, only the failed child restarts, which suits independent investigations that share no intermediate state. Under `one_for_all`, the supervisor stops and restarts every child in the group, which suits coupled work whose partial results lose their meaning when one member fails. @Fig-vol3-supervisor-tree-isolation contrasts the two policies. A caller worker building against a draft interface cannot keep its candidate if the interface worker restarts from a different design. A **restart intensity**\index{Restart intensity!definition} bound, a maximum number of restarts within a declared window, turns a repeatedly failing child into an escalated failure of its supervisor rather than an unbounded retry loop. For agents, each restart is a newly admitted attempt with its own reservation, it starts from recorded inputs rather than the failed child's context, and stopping its siblings follows the cancellation protocol of @sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure, which leaves the earlier attempt's unresolved operations with their owners.

::: {#fig-vol3-supervisor-tree-isolation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree**: Under the one-for-one policy (a), only the failed worker restarts, as a newly admitted attempt with its own reservation, while its siblings continue. Under the one-for-all policy (b), the supervisor stops the coupled siblings through the cancellation protocol and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs, because the caller's partial work has lost its meaning. Either supervisor that exceeds its declared restart intensity stops restarting and escalates the failure to its parent." fig-alt="A parent supervisor box above two cards. Card a, one_for_one: a supervisor with three worker children; the middle worker is marked failed and has an arrow labeled restart to a new attempt box with its own reservation, while the other two are marked continues. Card b, one_for_all: a supervisor with interface, caller, and test children; caller is marked failed, interface and test are marked stopped, and arrows from all three lead to one box labeled group restarts, new attempts from recorded inputs. A dashed arrow from supervisor b to the parent is labeled restart intensity exceeded, escalate."}
![](images/svg/supervisor_tree_isolation.svg)
:::

::: {#chk-17-amdahl-concurrency .callout-checkpoint title="Evaluating multi-agent coordination topologies"}

- [ ] **Dependency vs. routing**: The interface and caller workers communicate only through their supervisor. Why can they still produce interdependent patches, and which of the three structures records that?
- [ ] **Critical-path estimate**: Using the durations in @tbl-vol3-multiagent-dag-schedule, estimate how much completion changes if $v_6$ takes 20 s less, and how much if $v_5$ takes 20 s less. Which node would you ask a team to speed up?
- [ ] **Worker-count screen**: With $f=0.9$ and the notebook's overhead $a=$ `{python} DelegationScreen.overhead_str` per extra worker, estimate the best worker count from $\sqrt{f/a}$ and the speedup ceiling $1/(1-f)$. Is it worth halving $a$ or halving $1-f$?
- [ ] **Aggregate admission**: Why can granting every child less than its parent's remaining budget still oversubscribe the task? What must happen atomically?
:::

The topology identifies where responsibility and evidence cross boundaries. The next step is to specify each crossing: what the worker receives, what it may spend and do, and what it must return.

## Typed Task Envelopes {#sec-vol3-multiagent-contracts}

A dependency edge says when a child may begin. The envelope says what the child may read, change, spend, and return. In the authentication-module migration, `worker_caller_01` needs the interface at `repo_base_01`, permission to modify designated callers, and an acceptance contract. A message asking it to “update the callers” explains the assignment; the runtime supplies the operational boundaries. The typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}) therefore extends across the delegation boundary without making the worker's interpretation authoritative. The envelope plays the role that a typed interface plays in a remote procedure call [@birrell1984rpc], where caller and callee agree on arguments, results, and failure semantics before any work crosses the boundary.

::: {#dfn-typed-task-envelope .callout-definition title="Typed task envelope"}

***Typed task envelope***\index{Typed task envelope!definition} is a versioned assignment record binding a child task to identified inputs, a scoped authority grant, resource and lifecycle limits, completion requirements, and a bounded return format.

1. **Significance**: The runtime checks the assignment's boundaries before admitting work and compares its return with the required evidence, and the bounded return caps how much of each child's work re-enters the coordinator's context as input tokens in every later turn.
2. **Distinction**: The envelope specifies an operational contract; a natural-language assignment explains the desired work within that contract.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a well-formed envelope as proof of authorization or completion. Both require checks against records outside the worker's control.

:::

### An assignment the runtime can enforce

The parent proposes the work, but the runtime authenticates the task relationship and resolves the grant and reservation. @Lst-vol3-task-envelope shows one illustrative envelope. Its identifiers name registry records, not actual repository commits or credentials. The referenced acceptance contract specifies the required caller behavior, checker versions and environment, and any review that must precede acceptance.

::: {#lst-vol3-task-envelope lst-cap="**Bounded Child Assignment**: The envelope identifies inputs, authority, resource ownership, acceptance requirements, and limits on the return."}

```json
{
  "task_id": "worker_caller_01",
  "parent_task_id": "migration_task_01",
  "envelope_version": "caller_assignment_v1",
  "dispatch_id": "caller_dispatch_01",
  "assignment": "Update the designated authentication callers.",
  "inputs": {"base_ref": "repo_base_01"},
  "authority": {"grant_ref": "caller_private_patch_grant_01"},
  "budget": {"reservation_ref": "caller_reservation_01"},
  "completion": {
    "contract_ref": "migration_accept_v1",
    "required_evidence": [
      "candidate_ref", "write_set_ref", "dependencies_ref",
      "check_report_ref", "usage_ref", "settlement_ref"
    ]
  },
  "return_limits": {
    "receipt_bytes": 8192,
    "optional_summary_tokens": 256,
    "artifact_references": 8
  }
}
```

:::

Each binding answers a different question. The task and dispatch identifiers correlate an assignment with its execution records, and the admission and operation-ledger rules already established prevent duplicate execution. The base reference identifies the repository version the worker receives; reads beyond that snapshot, such as a package service or a clock, need their own version or observation records.

The grant identifies allowed operations and their data and target scope. For this child it permits designated caller edits in a private workspace, scoped repository reads, and bounded local checks, and withholds external publication; the grant scopes each tool's arguments as well as its name. The reservation identifies consumable allocations and their current accounting, such as token and tool-call allowances, while deadlines and lease validity live in the task and grant records as lifecycle conditions. The runtime resolves these records before admission and checks them as work proceeds, so editing the envelope enlarges nothing. Descendant authority and shared budget accounting are developed in @sec-vol3-multiagent-authority.

Completion requirements tell the runtime what evidence it needs. Some admit automated checks; others require identified human review or remain explicitly unresolved, and a test result establishes an outcome for a particular candidate, checker, and environment. The return limits are operational requirements too: they cap the receipt and its optional explanation and leave large artifacts outside the coordinator's context.

### A receipt separates evidence from explanation

The return in @lst-vol3-task-receipt refers to the same assignment and illustrates a candidate ready for integration review, which is one step short of an accepted change. The responsible runtime services populate or authenticate every field under `runtime`, so a worker's assertion placed under that key remains an assertion.

::: {#lst-vol3-task-receipt lst-cap="**Bounded Child Receipt**: Runtime records and a worker-authored explanation remain distinct; candidate readiness does not authorize publication."}

```json
{
  "task_id": "worker_caller_01",
  "envelope_version": "caller_assignment_v1",
  "dispatch_id": "caller_dispatch_01",
  "return_status": "complete",
  "runtime": {
    "status": "candidate_ready",
    "base_ref": "repo_base_01",
    "candidate_ref": "caller_candidate_01",
    "write_set_ref": "caller_writes_01",
    "dependencies_ref": "caller_dependencies_01",
    "check_report_ref": "caller_checks_01",
    "usage_ref": "caller_usage_01",
    "settlement_ref": "caller_settlement_01"
  },
  "worker_claims": {
    "summary": "Updated the designated callers for the migration."
  }
}
```

:::

The write-set record comes from the candidate's actual changes rather than the worker's memory of its edits. The dependency record identifies observed reads and versions, manifests, configuration, and external assumptions, with explicit coverage limits. The checker report names the exact candidate, checks, environment, outcomes, and missing assessments. Those records let the coordinator distinguish a locally passing candidate from a claim of success. If the runtime cannot obtain required evidence, the return reports `evidence_unavailable` or another declared incomplete status rather than `complete`.

Usage and settlement answer different questions from candidate quality. The usage record accounts for charged and reserved work. The settlement record distinguishes a stop acknowledgment, confirmed resource release, and unresolved operations with retained owners and possible charges. A `complete` return carries the required receipt evidence, and settlement of every operation is a separate status. These distinctions carry the weight when the parent cancels a branch in @sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure.

Return bounds preserve the evidence those decisions need. Optional prose may be shortened or omitted, with the omission recorded, while required identities, statuses, and evidence references pass intact. Large evidence belongs in access-controlled, versioned artifacts whose references fit the return contract. If the mandatory receipt still exceeds its bound, the runtime returns an explicit size failure and preserves the evidence for a separately authorized retrieval, which itself needs permission, budget, and an available artifact.

### References reduce copying only when reads remain selective

Passing the repository reference lets the child retrieve the files its assignment needs instead of receiving every file in advance. The saving is real only after counting the text that retrieval later returns, including any retrieved text re-sent on later turns.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-multiagent-reference-passing
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ REFERENCE-PASSING INPUT COST (LEGO)
# │ Context: @nbk-vol3-multiagent-reference-reads below.
# │ Goal: Count repository input after the child follows a reference.
# │ Show: Pasted, selectively retrieved, and fully retrieved input totals.
# │ How: Each supplied token is charged once at an illustrative input price.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_usd, USD

class RefPassing:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical repository-delivery inputs) ─────────────────
    workers = 6
    slice_tokens = 48_000
    envelope_ref_tokens = 350
    files_read_tokens = 3_600
    input_price_per_mtok = 3 * USD

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Charge each supplied token once) ──────────────────────
    pasted_tokens = workers * slice_tokens
    ref_tokens = workers * (envelope_ref_tokens + files_read_tokens)
    full_read_tokens = workers * (envelope_ref_tokens + slice_tokens)
    pasted_usd = pasted_tokens / 1_000_000 * input_price_per_mtok
    ref_usd = ref_tokens / 1_000_000 * input_price_per_mtok
    ratio = pasted_tokens / ref_tokens
    read_fraction = files_read_tokens / slice_tokens
    breakeven_read_tokens = slice_tokens - envelope_ref_tokens  # reads at which the saving vanishes

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Selective and full-retrieval ordering) ──────────────────
    check(0 < ref_tokens < pasted_tokens < full_read_tokens, "Input ordering")
    check(full_read_tokens - pasted_tokens == workers * envelope_ref_tokens, "Full retrieval retains the envelope overhead")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    workers_str = fmt_int(workers)
    slice_str = fmt_int(slice_tokens)
    envelope_ref_str = fmt_int(envelope_ref_tokens)
    files_read_str = fmt_int(files_read_tokens)
    input_price_str = fmt_usd(input_price_per_mtok, precision=0)
    pasted_str = fmt_int(pasted_tokens)
    ref_str = fmt_int(ref_tokens)
    full_read_str = fmt_int(full_read_tokens)
    pasted_usd_str = fmt_usd(pasted_usd, precision=3)
    ref_usd_str = fmt_usd(ref_usd, precision=3)
    ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio, precision=1)
    read_fraction_str = fmt_percent(read_fraction, precision=1, style="prose")
    breakeven_read_str = fmt_int(breakeven_read_tokens)
```

::: {#nbk-vol3-multiagent-reference-reads .callout-notebook title="Price the reads after the handoff"}

**Problem**: Each of `{python} RefPassing.workers_str` children receives either a `{python} RefPassing.slice_str`-token repository slice or a `{python} RefPassing.envelope_ref_str`-token reference envelope followed by `{python} RefPassing.files_read_str` tokens of retrieved content. With all other inputs equal, no cache discount, and a hypothetical `{python} RefPassing.input_price_str` per million input tokens, how much repository-delivery input does the reference save?

**Math**: Pasting costs `{python} RefPassing.workers_str` $\times$ `{python} RefPassing.slice_str` $=$ `{python} RefPassing.pasted_str` tokens, or `{python} RefPassing.pasted_usd_str`. The reference costs `{python} RefPassing.workers_str` $\times$ (`{python} RefPassing.envelope_ref_str` $+$ `{python} RefPassing.files_read_str`) $=$ `{python} RefPassing.ref_str` tokens, or `{python} RefPassing.ref_usd_str`, a `{python} RefPassing.ratio_mult_str` reduction. If every child instead reads the full slice, the reference design consumes `{python} RefPassing.full_read_str` tokens and loses its saving.

**Systems insight**: The saving is set by how much each child reads, not by the reference itself. Here each child reads `{python} RefPassing.read_fraction_str` of its slice, and the reference stays cheaper until a child reads `{python} RefPassing.breakeven_read_str` tokens, so the design lever is a narrow, well-indexed assignment. The same accounting extends to the full bill once retrieval calls, repeated context, verification, and waits are added.
:::

Prefix caching needs compatible delivered token prefixes, model state, and cache namespace, as established in context engineering, so a shared artifact reference saves prefill only when the delivered tokens also match. The envelope's contribution is narrower: each child receives a bounded assignment and returns identified evidence without forwarding its entire transcript.

The caller receipt now gives the parent a candidate, its base, and the evidence supporting it. Whether that candidate is safe to combine with `worker_interface_01`'s changes is a separate question, which the next section answers by using these records to validate concurrent integration, including dependencies between patches that write different files.

## Optimistic Concurrency Control {#sec-vol3-multiagent-concurrency}

The authentication migration assigns `worker_interface_01` to change an interface and `worker_caller_01` to update a caller. Both start from `repo_base_01`. The interface worker finishes first, and its accepted change becomes `repo_head_02`. The caller worker writes a different file, so a textual merge succeeds without conflict, and its patch still calls the old interface. Separate write paths prevented one collision and left the dependency behind the caller's work unchecked.

**Optimistic concurrency control (OCC)**\index{Optimistic concurrency control!definition} allows work to proceed privately, then validates the conditions required for publication [@kung1981optimistic]. For a delegated code change, those conditions include both the candidate's dependencies and its acceptance evidence. The runtime separates private editing from integration instead of holding a repository-wide lock throughout model generation, which exposes parallelism and makes revalidation and discarded work part of the coordination tax.

### Private workspaces do not provide containment

A shared working directory exposes three distinct hazards. A **lost update**\index{Lost update!definition} occurs when two workers read the same file, deliberate for seconds or minutes, and write in turn, so the later write silently replaces the earlier one; each write is a valid filesystem operation, so nothing below the runtime detects the loss. A **torn dependency read**\index{Torn dependency read!definition} occurs when a worker runs its tests after a peer has written a changed interface but before it has updated the callers, so the test evaluates an intermediate mixture that no worker proposed. *Tool-lock contention* occurs when concurrent version-control or build commands collide on the tool's own lock files, such as Git's `.git/index.lock`, so one worker's command fails even when the two workers' edits never overlap.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-multiagent-write-collision
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WRITE COLLISIONS IN A SHARED WORKSPACE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-multiagent-write-collision and the prose that follows it
# │          in @sec-vol3-multiagent-concurrency.
# │ Goal: Show that uniform, independent write sets collide at small fleet sizes.
# │ Show: Collision probability for two and eight workers, and the smallest
# │       fleet for which a collision is more likely than not.
# │ How: Exact sequential product of disjoint-draw probabilities, checked
# │      against the exponential (birthday) approximation.
# │ Note: Hypothetical repository and write-set sizes, not measured workloads.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import comb, exp
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class WriteCollision:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical repository and write sets) ─────────────────
    files = 1_000
    writes_per_worker = 10
    small_fleet = 2
    large_fleet = 8
    max_fleet = 16

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Probability that N write sets are pairwise disjoint) ─
    no_collision = {}
    approx_no_collision = {}
    for fleet in range(1, max_fleet + 1):
        disjoint = 1.0
        for earlier in range(1, fleet):
            disjoint *= comb(files - earlier * writes_per_worker, writes_per_worker) / comb(files, writes_per_worker)
        no_collision[fleet] = disjoint
        approx_no_collision[fleet] = exp(-fleet * (fleet - 1) * writes_per_worker**2 / (2 * files))
    small_collision = 1 - no_collision[small_fleet]
    large_collision = 1 - no_collision[large_fleet]
    even_odds_fleet = None
    for fleet in range(max_fleet, 0, -1):
        if no_collision[fleet] < 0.5:
            even_odds_fleet = fleet

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Prose claims) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(no_collision[1] - 1) < 1e-12, "One worker cannot collide")
    check(abs(no_collision[large_fleet] - approx_no_collision[large_fleet]) < 0.01, "Approximation must track the exact product here")
    check(0.09 < small_collision < 0.11, "Two workers collide about one time in ten")
    check(large_collision > 0.9, "Eight workers collide with high probability")
    check(even_odds_fleet == 5, "Five workers first exceed even odds")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    files_str = fmt_int(files)
    writes_str = fmt_int(writes_per_worker)
    small_fleet_str = fmt_int(small_fleet)
    large_fleet_str = fmt_int(large_fleet)
    even_odds_fleet_str = fmt_int(even_odds_fleet)
    small_collision_str = fmt_percent(small_collision, precision=1, style="prose")
    small_disjoint_str = fmt_percent(1 - small_collision, precision=1, style="prose")
    large_collision_str = fmt_percent(large_collision, precision=1, style="prose")
```

These collisions arrive at small fleet sizes. Suppose a repository holds $F$ files and each of $N$ workers writes $w$ of them, chosen uniformly and independently. Worker $k+1$ avoids every earlier write set only if it draws all $w$ files from the $F-kw$ files that earlier workers left untouched, so the probability that no two write sets intersect is

$$
P(\text{no shared write})=\prod_{k=1}^{N-1}\frac{\binom{F-kw}{w}}{\binom{F}{w}}\approx\exp\left(-\frac{N(N-1)w^2}{2F}\right).
$$ {#eq-vol3-multiagent-write-collision}

@Eq-vol3-multiagent-write-collision is the birthday bound applied to write sets. Its exponent grows with the number of worker pairs, not the number of workers. With `{python} WriteCollision.files_str` files and `{python} WriteCollision.writes_str` writes per worker, `{python} WriteCollision.small_fleet_str` workers share at least one file with probability `{python} WriteCollision.small_collision_str`, `{python} WriteCollision.even_odds_fleet_str` workers are the smallest fleet for which a shared write is more likely than not, and `{python} WriteCollision.large_fleet_str` workers collide with probability `{python} WriteCollision.large_collision_str`. Uniform access is the favorable case. Real edits concentrate on manifests, configuration, and core interfaces, which makes a collision more likely than this estimate. Isolation is therefore the default for concurrent writers rather than an optimization reserved for large fleets.

A private workspace gives each worker a stable base and a place for its own changes. The runtime records the base commit and returns an immutable candidate artifact rather than accepting a mutable directory path as the result.

Git worktrees implement one form of working-directory separation. Linked worktrees have their own checked-out files, index, and `HEAD`, while sharing repository storage and much administrative state. Checkout contents, build products, caches, and filesystem behavior determine their storage and setup costs. Copy-on-write filesystems offer a different sharing mechanism, whose costs and reset contract are established in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling.

This separation organizes files; the sandbox and tool gateway provide the security boundary. A worker with unrestricted filesystem or Git access can reach shared repository state or another worktree, so the gateway enforces write scope and keeps integration authority outside the workers. Tests also need scoped temporary directories, ports, credentials, and external resources where those can interfere. Discarding a worktree removes local candidate state and leaves any request already accepted by an external service in place.

### Validate dependencies before publishing a candidate

The integration service consumes the task envelope and receipt from @sec-vol3-multiagent-contracts. It resolves `runtime.base_ref` and `runtime.candidate_ref`, authenticates their task lineage, and independently derives the candidate's changed paths for `runtime.write_set_ref` rather than trusting the worker's claimed write set. The service also needs `runtime.dependencies_ref`, describing which source versions and environmental assumptions the result relied on and the coverage of that record.

That record can include files read through mediated tools, interface definitions, dependency manifests, configuration, and versioned external inputs. A search result may depend on the absence of a matching file as well as on the files returned; logging only opened files misses that dependency. Runtime instrumentation and declared task inputs provide that coverage; a model-written summary does not. Where coverage is incomplete, the service refreshes or reruns affected work against the current base and treats an empty dependency list as unknown rather than independent. The historical observation remains part of the trace, but no longer establishes a current precondition, following @sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot.

Let $C_{\mathrm{base}}$ identify the worker's base, $C_i$ its returned candidate, and $C_{\mathrm{head}}$ the integration head captured for this attempt. The service compares relevant dependency versions at the base and head before deciding whether the worker's result can be reused. Disjoint writes are evidence about textual composition only; behavioral independence needs the dependency comparison, whether the hunks are disjoint or overlapping. If a dependency changed, the affected result needs revalidation or regeneration against the new condition before integration can continue.

Once dependencies have been addressed, the service constructs an immutable integration candidate $C_{\mathrm{candidate}}$. When the head still equals the base, this can be the worker's existing candidate. Otherwise, it combines the current head with the proposed change in a private staging workspace. A merge conflict or an unresolved dependency can justify a bounded reconciliation task. Its output is another proposal, not a privileged exception to validation.

Every candidate, including the unchanged-head fast-forward case, passes the required scope and acceptance checks before publication. The resulting evidence binds the exact candidate to `migration_accept_v1`, checker versions, and relevant environment inputs. A check against the worker's original branch covers that branch, so a newly merged candidate is checked again. Candidate execution remains untrusted, so the protected assessment boundary from @sec-vol3-evaluation applies, and passing the declared checks establishes their scoped result.

Publication then uses an atomic expected-head update. The integration service advances the target only if it still equals the captured $C_{\mathrm{head}}$ and the candidate's current publication guards remain satisfied. This is the repository counterpart of the conditional-update contract in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-schemas. Git's `update-ref` with an expected old object ID supplies the reference comparison and update; task cancellation, grants, dependency coverage, and acceptance evidence are the runtime's guards. The runtime must coordinate those guards with publication so that revocation and a commit have a defined order, with every writer using the same integration boundary. Relevant dependencies outside the repository head are pinned or protected by their own action-time version contract, because an earlier freshness check leaves that race open.

If another writer changes the head before this update, the attempt returns to dependency validation, constructs the candidate for the new head, and establishes evidence for that exact candidate rather than retrying with the new expected value. Reusing an unchanged immutable candidate's evidence requires the same checked inputs and contract to remain applicable. An uncertain publication response also requires reconciliation of the authoritative publication record before the runtime reports success or retries the effect.

@Fig-vol3-occ-worktrees places the protocol beside the workspaces and history it governs, and @lst-vol3-occ-commit condenses it into the control flow of an integration service. Every exit other than publication returns an explicit status to the supervisor, and a moved head sends the attempt back to dependency validation rather than to a retried update.

::: {#lst-vol3-occ-commit lst-cap="**Guarded Integration of a Worker Candidate**: The service revalidates dependencies against the captured head, checks the exact candidate, and publishes with an expected-head update under the task's publication guard."}

```python
def integrate(repo, task, receipt, contract, max_attempts):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        head = repo.read_ref(TARGET)                          # C_head for this attempt
        stale = changed_dependencies(receipt.dependencies_ref, receipt.base_ref, head)
        if stale:
            return request_revision(task, stale, head)        # regenerate, then return
        if head == receipt.base_ref:
            candidate = receipt.candidate_ref                 # fast-forward case
        else:
            candidate = stage_merge(head, receipt.candidate_ref)
            if candidate is None:
                return request_reconciliation(task, head)     # another proposal
        evidence = run_protected_checks(contract, candidate)  # binds this exact candidate
        if not evidence.accepted:
            return reject(task, candidate, evidence)
        with publication_guard(task) as guard:                # cancellation, grants, lineage
            if not guard.eligible:
                return withdrawn(task)
            outcome = repo.update_ref(TARGET, candidate, expected=head)
        if outcome.uncertain:
            return reconcile_publication(task, candidate)     # never blind-retry the effect
        if outcome.applied:
            return published(task, candidate, evidence)
        # head moved: loop back to dependency validation for the new head
    return unresolved(task, reason="integration_attempts_exhausted")
```

:::

::: {#fig-vol3-occ-worktrees fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Private Workspaces and Guarded Publication**: Linked worktrees (a) give each worker its own files, index, and HEAD while sharing repository storage; the sandbox around each one, not the worktree, scopes its writes. The caller edits files the interface change never touched (b), so the staged merge is textually clean even though the caller relies on the interface as of $C_{\mathrm{base}}$. Publication (c) therefore revalidates dependencies at the captured head, checks the exact integration candidate, and advances the target only if the head is unchanged and the publication guard holds. A moved head returns the attempt to validation, and every other exit returns an explicit status." fig-alt="Three panels. Panel a: a shared repository storage box linked to an interface worktree and a caller worktree, each holding files, index, and HEAD inside a dashed sandbox with scoped writes, and a note that this separation is not a security boundary. Panel b: commit C base, repo_base_01, with an interface-change arrow to C head, repo_head_02, and a caller-edits branch to worker candidate C i marked as relying on the old interface; C head and C i both lead to integration candidate C candidate by a staged merge. Panel c: four steps in a row, revalidate dependencies at head, build candidate, protected checks on the exact candidate, and atomic update with expected head and guard held, ending in published; each step has a red exit, request revision, request reconciliation, reject, and reconcile outcome, and a dashed arrow labeled head moved returns from the update step to revalidation."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-occ-worktrees.svg)
:::

@Tbl-vol3-occ-dependency-trace follows the caller patch through this protocol. The identifiers name hypothetical artifacts, not literal Git hashes or observed results.

| Integration boundary                            | Evidence available                                                     | Required decision                                             |
|:------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Both workers start at `repo_base_01`            | Caller depends on the original interface                               | Keep each candidate private                                   |
| Interface change becomes `repo_head_02`         | Caller writes are separate, but its interface dependency changed       | Revalidate or regenerate affected caller work                 |
| Revised caller candidate passes required checks | Results identify the exact combined candidate and checked inputs       | Attempt guarded publication against `repo_head_02`            |
| Head changes before publication                 | Candidate evidence was established for the earlier integration attempt | Return to validation; do not overwrite the intervening change |

: **A Clean Merge with a Stale Dependency**: Publication requires current dependency support and exact-candidate evidence, even when the workers edit different files. {#tbl-vol3-occ-dependency-trace}

Repeated invalidation can consume the benefit of delegation. Bounded retries, backoff, or a serialized integration queue limit contention, and a deadline or exhausted allowance ends the attempt with an explicit unresolved result. When invalidation is frequent, the better fix is the partition: scheduling interface changes before dependent caller work removes the conflict that adding workers would multiply.

### External resources need an enforcing ownership boundary

Repository staging contains only repository state. Operations on a shared database or remote test service use the endpoint's conditional-update, ownership, and repeat contracts, and a failed repository integration rolls none of them back. The ownership and effect-settlement distinctions in @sec-vol3-persistence-migration remain in force across worker boundaries.

For a resource that cannot be branched and merged, such as a shared database schema, a remote test environment, or a reserved device, the runtime must choose when to establish exclusion. A **pessimistic lease**\index{Pessimistic lease!definition} acquires ownership before the worker acts. A conflicting worker then waits instead of discarding work, at the price of serializing every holder of that resource and tying progress to lease renewal. *Optimistic control* lets workers proceed and validates at publication. Parallelism is high, a rejected attempt discards its trajectory, and an external effect already performed stays performed. That last property decides most cases. Optimistic control fits private, discardable candidates; an operation whose effect lands outside the runtime needs exclusion established at the resource before the effect is sent. @Tbl-vol3-concurrency-controls summarizes the trade-off.

| Control                                   | Exclusion established                            | Cost of a conflict                       | Parallelism                              | Fits                                         | Residual hazard                                                       |
|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Pessimistic lease with fencing            | Before acting, at the resource                   | Waiting; no work discarded               | Serialized per resource                  | Non-mergeable resources and external effects | Stalled holders; expiry needs a resource-side fence                   |
| Optimistic validation at publication      | At publication, against the captured head        | Discarded trajectory and repeated checks | Workers proceed concurrently             | Private, discardable candidates              | Repeated invalidation under contention                                |
| Optimistic validation with reconciliation | At publication, followed by a bounded merge task | Reconciliation work and a new check      | Concurrent, plus the reconciliation work | Coupled changes that usually compose         | A reconciled candidate is another proposal that needs full validation |

: **Where Exclusion Is Established**: Leases pay in waiting before the work; optimistic control pays in discarded or reconciled work afterward, which only private candidates can afford. {#tbl-vol3-concurrency-controls}

A resource using authenticated fencing generations rejects requests from an older ownership generation after the newer generation has been installed or established at that resource. It must permit distinct authorized operations from the current holder; rejecting every token less than or equal to the last accepted token would reject that holder's second operation. Repeated delivery of one operation is a separate deduplication problem [@kleppmann2017designing].

A monotone generation number orders owners; it does not measure time. Until a newer generation reaches the resource, expiry of the old lease needs an explicit lease-validity check under the resource's timing and ownership contract, and the handoff establishes the new fence at each relevant boundary before relying on exclusion. Only an authenticated grant installs a generation, and a gateway check governs requests it has not yet forwarded. The runtime retains unresolved operations and charges under their existing identities rather than assigning them away with the workspace. @Sec-vol3-appendix-systems-fencing works the delayed-writer history before and after fence installation, separating lease expiry from resource-side exclusion.

Private execution, dependency validation, and guarded publication let the runtime control how concurrent proposals affect shared state. Whether several proposals are independent evidence of correctness is a separate question: workers can follow the protocol and still recommend the same mistaken change, which is the ensemble problem considered next.

## Correlated Ensemble Failures {#sec-vol3-multiagent-consensus}

Validating a worker's dependencies establishes which candidate its evidence describes. How much confidence several workers' matching conclusions deserve is a different question. In the migration example, reviewers may all accept the caller patch because they all assume the old interface remains available, adding approvals without checking the dependency that matters. This is a **correlated failure**\index{Correlated failure!multi-agent definition}: reviewers err on the same inputs, so agreement is worth what their joint error model says it is worth.

### Shared difficulty and conditional independence

Readers from systems courses bring two traditions to this problem. Condorcet's jury theorem [@condorcet1785essai] states that if independent voters are each correct with probability above one half, a majority becomes correct with probability approaching one as voters are added. N-modular redundancy applies the same arithmetic to hardware, masking a faulty replica by majority vote [@vonneumann1956probabilistic]. Both depend on the same premise, that voters fail independently given the truth. @Tbl-vol3-nmr-vs-review-ensembles contrasts where that premise comes from in each setting.

| Question                | Replicated hardware under majority vote                      | Model reviewers under majority vote                                            |
|:------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Source of independence  | Physically separate faults such as particle strikes and wear | Must be established; shared training, prompts, and inputs can correlate errors |
| What a replica checks   | The same deterministic computation                           | A judgment about a candidate whose difficulty is shared by every reviewer      |
| What adding voters buys | Majority error falls rapidly when faults are independent     | Gain depends on the joint error model and may level off at a floor             |

: **Redundancy with and without Independent Faults**: Majority voting inherits its guarantee from independent failures, which replicated hardware has by construction and model reviewers must be shown to have. {#tbl-vol3-nmr-vs-review-ensembles}

Consider binary reviews of candidates known to violate a specified acceptance criterion. Let $X_j=1$ mean reviewer $j$ nevertheless approves, and let $p$ be a reviewer's false-approval probability over this candidate population. If $M$ reviewers have independent errors with the same probability $p$, their number of false approvals $K$ is binomial. For odd $M$, majority false approval has probability

$$
P(K>M/2)=\sum_{k=(M+1)/2}^{M}\binom{M}{k}p^k(1-p)^{M-k}.
$$

Independence must be stated relative to the information held fixed. With an identical fixed input, independently randomized calls to the same fixed model can produce conditionally independent outputs. Across different candidates, however, some defects are much harder for that model to detect than others.
